newsitem.title: VATICAN: Netanyahu invites Pope to make Israel visit soon.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu invites Pope to make Israel visit soon.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu discussed the Middle East peace process with Pope John Paul on Monday and invited him to make an historic visit to the Holy Land "as soon as possible".
"We look forward to receiving you in Jerusalem," Netanyahu said as he was leaving the Roman Catholic Pontiff's study after a 20-minute private audience.
The Polish Pope responded: "God Bless Israel".
No date for an eventual visit was given but a Vatican statement said Netanyahu had invited the Pope "to make a visit to the Holy Land as soon as possible".
In 1994, the Pope accepted an open invitation made by the late Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin.

The Pope, who has often said he wants to visit Holy Land sites by the year 2000, last year also accepted an invitation by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat to visit Christ's birthplace in Bethlehem at the turn of the millennium.
A trip to the Holy Land, one of the 76-year-old Pope's cherished dreams, would be the first by a Roman Catholic leader since Paul VI visited the Holy Land in 1964.
The Pope met Netanyahu a day after the Israeli leader and Arafat agreed at a meeting in Switzerland to convene again on Thursday for detailed talks on extending Palestinian self-rule.
The Vatican statement described the talks as cordial and said Netanyahu had briefed the Pope on the status of the Middle East Peace process.

The Pope told Netanyahu he hoped the region could become a place where "Jews, Christians, Moslems, Israelis and Arabs, believers and non-believers can create and consolidate a concrete peace in respect of everyone's rights and dignity".
The Vatican and Israel ended nearly 2,000 years of often hostile Catholic-Jewish relations in 1994 when they established full diplomatic relations.
The two sides have since been working towards agreement on issues regarding the legal status of the Catholic Church and its clerical hierarchy in the Jewish state.

The statement said Netanyahu promised the Pope "to move ahead along the same path" as his predecessors towards reaching an agreement on the legal status of the Catholic Church in the land where Christ lived and died.
The Vatican statement did not say whether the two had discussed the divisive issue of the status of Jerusalem, which Israel declared its "united and eternal capital" in 1980.
The Vatican, which like most other countries keeps its embassy in or near Tel Aviv, wants international guarantees protecting Jerusalem as sacred for Christians, Moslems and Jews.

Arafat said during a visit to Rome last year that Jerusalem would either make or break Middle East peace. Palestinians view East Jerusalem, which Israel captured in the 1967 Six Day War, as the capital of a future state.

The Pontiff, who has suffered a string of health problems over the last few years, appeared in good form during the picture-taking session of the audience. He joked and chatted easily with Netanyahu, his wife Sara and their delegation.
"You look like a Polish girl," he joked with Netanyahu's wife, who is of Polish origin.
The Pontiff also drew a loud laugh from Netanyahu when he noticed that there were too many people to his left and not enough on his right for the official photograph.
"Not only the left," the Pope said. Netanyahu, who is from the conservative Likud party, laughed heartily and repeated. "Yes, not only on the left".
